US$350,000 for the top early-stage medtech startup, and applications close on 1 December.

MedTech Innovator 2027 is a five-month accelerator run by the non-profit MedTech Innovator for companies building medical devices, diagnostics and digital health products. It ends in a public prize competition where the early-stage track plays for US$350K and the mid-stage track for US$250K, with more than US$700K in prizes overall. Along the way you get matched with industry mentors, meet investors, and showcase at The MedTech Conference.

Indian startups can apply as long as they have a clear plan for the US market. You should be early to mid-stage with clinical validation under way or coming up, and a founder or C-suite leader has to commit to the full five months.

The catch many founders miss: applying is free, but if you are selected there is a US$15,000 programme fee, payable in cash or as a US$50K SAFE, and some specialty tracks require the SAFE. Scholarships exist, so ask. The deadline is on US time, so submit by 30 November in India to be safe.

Did you know IIT Delhi's incubator gives grants of up to ₹1 crore to startups from the idea stage onward, with no fixed deadline?

FITT, the Foundation for Innovation and Technology Transfer at IIT Delhi, runs the institute's technology transfer and incubation work. Startups it takes into incubation can receive grants anywhere from ₹4 lakh to ₹1 crore to refine an idea, build a prototype or test the market. Alongside the money, you get access to IIT Delhi's labs and infrastructure, scale-up support, and help raising capital from seed rounds onward through FITT's network.

The grant is not a standalone open call. You reach it by applying for incubation through FITT's standing application, and once in, you submit a fund-utilisation plan tied to clear goals and spend the money according to FITT's guidelines.

One practical tip: these grants are usually drawn from government schemes FITT runs, such as TIDE 2.0 and BIRAC BIG, so the terms of whichever scheme matches you will apply. FITT says the amount depends on your plan and on the funds available, and incubation fees are not published, so ask FITT about both before you commit.

text:
You do not need a registered company to get up to ₹20 lakh from the Government of India for your prototype.

PRISM is a scheme of the Department of Scientific & Industrial Research (DSIR) under the Ministry of Science & Technology. It helps Indian individual innovators turn an idea into a working prototype, model or process. Category I projects costing up to ₹5 lakh can get the lesser of ₹2 lakh or 90% of the cost for proof-of-concept work. Category II projects costing ₹5 to 35 lakh can get the lesser of ₹20 lakh or 90% of the cost for fabrication, testing, patenting and technology transfer. It is non-dilutive, so you give up no equity.

Students, independent innovators and researchers can apply, as can technology providers building solutions for MSME clusters. Priority areas include green tech, clean energy, smart materials, waste to wealth, affordable healthcare, and water and sewage management.

The step founders often skip: there is no online form on the official pages. Proposals go through DSIR's Technology and Innovation Outreach Centres, such as Venture Center in Pune, so contact your nearest centre for the current format and intake schedule. Remember you must fund the remaining 10% of the project cost yourself.
